title: Tarte Tatin aux Tomates
subtitle: Upside-down caramelised tomato tart with thyme and Dijon mustard
excerpt: Tarte tatin aux tomates applies the upside-down caramelised technique of the original tarte tatin to tomatoes. The tomatoes are slowly reduced in the tin with olive oil, sugar, and thyme until almost jammy, then topped with puff pastry and baked. Turned out, it reveals a glossy, caramelised tomato top.
sourceNotes: A savoury adaptation of the Tarte Tatin concept from the Loire Valley. Using the tatin technique for vegetables became fashionable in French restaurant cooking during the 1980s and 1990s.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tomato base can be prepared up to 1 day ahead. Add the pastry and bake on the day.

content.text: This tart works best with small, firm tomatoes (cherry, vine, or plum) that hold their shape when cooked. Beef or large salad tomatoes become too watery and collapse. The Dijon mustard is not traditional in the original tatin but works perfectly here: spread over the pastry before placing it on top of the tomatoes, it adds sharpness to the sweet caramelised base.

Heat the olive oil in a 25 to 28 cm ovenproof frying pan (cast-iron or heavy-based) over medium-high heat. Add the sugar and let it begin to caramelise for 1 minute. Add the balsamic vinegar, garlic, and thyme.

Pack the tomatoes cut-side down in a single layer in the pan. Season with salt and pepper. Cook over medium heat without stirring for 20 to 25 minutes until the tomatoes have softened and the juices have reduced to a sticky glaze. The base of the pan should look thick and caramelised, not watery.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Roll the puff pastry to a circle slightly larger than the pan. Spread the Dijon mustard across the pastry. Place the pastry mustard-side down on top of the tomatoes, tucking the edges in around the tomatoes.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until the pastry is deep golden and well risen. Remove from the oven and rest for 5 minutes. Place a large plate over the pan and carefully invert. Serve warm.

items.symptom: Tomatoes are watery and the tart collapses when turned out
items.cause: Tomatoes were not reduced enough before the pastry was added
items.fix: The tomato juices must be cooked down to a thick, sticky glaze before topping with pastry. If the pan still has liquid, continue cooking uncovered to evaporate it.

items.symptom: Pastry is not fully cooked underneath
items.cause: Pan was too full of liquid which steamed the pastry rather than letting it bake
items.fix: See above: reduce the tomatoes properly first. Also ensure the oven is fully preheated before the tart goes in.

content.text: Serve warm, not hot, with a salad and some soft goat's cheese crumbled over the top. The acidity of the cheese cuts through the sweetness of the caramelised tomatoes.
